positions/progressive-covenantalism/altN: "Via media" between covenant theology and dispensationalism
positions/progressive-covenantalism/oneL: The biblical covenants (creation, Noah, Abraham, Israel, David, new covenant) unfold progressively and all find their fulfilment in Christ; Israel’s promises are fulfilled in him and his new covenant people, which is a regenerate community.
positions/progressive-covenantalism/core: A covenant with creation in Adam; each later covenant builds on earlier ones toward Christ.
Israel is a typological pattern fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel, rather than replaced by the church.
The new covenant is new in nature, not only administration: all its members know the Lord (Jer 31:34).
The land promise is typological of the new creation.
Believer’s baptism follows from the regenerate nature of the new covenant community.
positions/progressive-covenantalism/orig: Set out by Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum in Kingdom through Covenant (2012; 2nd ed. 2018) and in Progressive Covenantalism (eds. Wellum and Brent Parker, 2016), building on D. A. Carson, Douglas Moo and New Covenant Theology.
positions/progressive-covenantalism/stro: It takes each covenant on its own terms in canonical sequence, the way biblical theology reads the Bible.
Christ as the true Israel (Matt 2:15; John 15:1) explains how Israel’s promises are fulfilled without a "replacement" of Jews by Gentiles.
It coherently grounds believer’s baptism and the regenerate church in Jeremiah 31.
Covenant theologians argue that warnings to new covenant members (Heb 6; 10) show the visible church is mixed, undermining the regenerate-membership claim.
Dispensationalists argue that typological fulfilment still amounts to supersessionism for ethnic Israel.
Some critics see it as a scholarly synthesis without confessional or ecclesial anchoring.
positions/progressive-covenantalism/resp: Proponents answer that warning passages are means by which God preserves true members rather than evidence of a mixed covenant.
They hold that ethnic Jews remain welcome in Christ with a possible future turning (Rom 11), so the view is "fulfilment" rather than "replacement".
positions/progressive-covenantalism/cons: Influential at Southern Baptist seminaries and in evangelical biblical-theology circles since 2012.
Reframed Reformed Baptist debates on covenant and baptism.
positions/law-gospel-distinction/name: Lutheran distinction of law and gospel
positions/law-gospel-distinction/oneLine: God’s Word speaks in two distinct ways: the law, which commands, exposes sin and condemns, and the gospel, which freely promises forgiveness for Christ’s sake; rightly distinguishing them is the heart of pastoral theology.
positions/law-gospel-distinction/coreCla: The law (wherever it appears in Scripture) demands and accuses; the gospel (wherever it appears) gives and promises.
Justification comes through the gospel received by faith alone, never through law-keeping.
Mixing the two produces either despair or self-righteousness; the preacher must apply law to the secure and gospel to the terrified.
The Christian is simul iustus et peccator: as sinner still under the law’s accusation, as believer free in Christ.
The Mosaic law as such was given to Israel; its moral content binds all as natural law.
positions/law-gospel-distinction/origin: Central to Luther’s Reformation breakthrough (c.1518–1525; How Christians Should Regard Moses, 1525; Galatians lectures 1531/1535); confessed in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531) and the Formula of Concord (1577); classically expounded by C. F. W. Walther, The Proper Distinction between Law and Gospel (lectures 1884–85).
positions/law-gospel-distinction/stronge: Paul contrasts "the letter" that kills with "the spirit" that gives life (2 Cor 3:6), and righteousness "of the law" with righteousness "of faith" (Rom 10:5–6).
It protects the gospel as sheer gift and gives pastors a practical tool for the troubled and the complacent.
It explains why the same commandment can terrify one hearer and guide another.
Reformed critics (and Karl Barth, who reversed the order to "gospel and law") argue it isolates law as merely negative and neglects law as gracious gift (Ps 119).
Catholic and Orthodox theologians see it as a dialectic foreign to the patristic vision of grace healing and transforming nature.
New Perspective scholars argue Paul’s "works of the law" concerned Jewish boundary markers more than human moral striving.
positions/law-gospel-distinction/respons: Lutherans answer that the law is good and holy in itself; it is sin that makes it accusing, and the Formula of Concord affirms its use for the regenerate.
They reply that the law–gospel distinction is not a philosophical dialectic but describes the two ways Scripture itself addresses the conscience.
positions/law-gospel-distinction/consequ: Shapes Lutheran preaching, catechesis and liturgy.
Generated the antinomian and Majoristic controversies within Lutheranism.
Influenced Reformed thought (e.g. Westminster’s covenant of works vs grace) and modern "gospel-centred" evangelicalism.
positions/three-uses-of-the-law/altNames: Third use of the law (tertius usus)
positions/three-uses-of-the-law/oneLine: God’s law has a civil use (restraining evil in society), a theological or pedagogical use (exposing sin and driving to Christ) and a third use as a guide and rule of life for believers.
positions/three-uses-of-the-law/coreClai: First use: the law restrains wickedness and preserves public order.
Second use: it convicts of sin and leads to Christ (Gal 3:24).
Third use: it instructs and exhorts the regenerate, who delight in it inwardly (Ps 1; Rom 7:22).
Reformed theology calls the third use "principal" (Calvin); Lutheran confessions affirm it while stressing the law still accuses.
positions/three-uses-of-the-law/origin: Melanchthon introduced the third use in the 1535 Loci communes (anticipated in his 1534 Colossians commentary); Calvin expounded the three uses in the Institutes (1539–1559) and Lutheranism confessed them in the Formula of Concord (1577).
positions/three-uses-of-the-law/stronges: Paul both says believers are "not under the law" and appeals to its commandments as guidance (Rom 13:8–10; Eph 6:2).
The new covenant writes the law on the heart (Jer 31:33), implying the law’s content remains the shape of the renewed life.
It avoids both legalism (law as way of salvation) and antinomianism (law as irrelevant to the saved).
Some Lutherans (e.g. Werner Elert, Gerhard Forde) argue that the law "always accuses" (lex semper accusat) and that a separate third use risks a new legalism.
New Covenant theologians say Christians are under the law of Christ rather than the Decalogue as such.
Antinomian critics hold that the indwelling Spirit, not an external code, guides the believer.
positions/three-uses-of-the-law/response: Defenders answer that the Spirit guides by means of the Word, which includes commandments, and that external guidance is necessary because believers remain sinners.
They point to the Formula of Concord itself, which affirms the third use while acknowledging the law’s accusing function in the believer.
positions/three-uses-of-the-law/conseque: Structures the Heidelberg Catechism (guilt, grace, gratitude) and Reformed ethics.
Basis of Decalogue-centred catechesis across Protestant traditions.
Continuing intra-Lutheran debate in the 20th century.
positions/antinomianism/oneLine: Because believers are wholly justified by grace and led by the Spirit, the law should not be preached to them as a rule or used to measure assurance; repentance and holiness spring from the gospel alone.
positions/antinomianism/coreClaims/0: Repentance is produced by the gospel of Christ’s love, not by preaching the law (Agricola).
positions/antinomianism/coreClaims/1: Assurance rests on Christ and the Spirit’s witness, not on evidences of sanctification (Hutchinson and the 1630s "free grace" party).
positions/antinomianism/coreClaims/2: Believers are "not under the law, but under grace" (Rom 6:14) and "dead to the law" (Rom 7:4).
positions/antinomianism/coreClaims/3: In its radical (often alleged rather than held) form: sin cannot harm the justified, so moral law is irrelevant.
positions/antinomianism/keyTexts/2: 1 Timothy 1:9 ("the law is not made for a righteous man")
positions/antinomianism/origin: The term was coined by Luther against Johann Agricola (1537–40); English antinomianism flourished in the 1630s–40s (John Eaton, Tobias Crisp) and in New England’s Free Grace controversy (1636–38); the label was later hurled at the Marrow men (1720), Wesley’s and Whitefield’s opponents, and modern "hyper-grace" preachers.
positions/antinomianism/strongestArgumen: Paul’s strongest statements on freedom from the law (Gal 2:19; Rom 7:4) seem to leave no room for the law as master of the believer.
Preaching the law to believers can produce anxiety and legalism, undermining assurance; the Free Grace party saw this in Puritan "preparationism".
Love and gratitude kindled by the gospel are a stronger motive for holiness than commands.
positions/antinomianism/strongestObjecti: Paul anticipates and rejects the inference "shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?" (Rom 6:1–2) and gives many commands to believers.
Luther argued that without the law sin is not known, so grace becomes meaningless; the Formula of Concord rejected antinomianism.
Private claims to the Spirit’s direct witness, detached from Scripture’s commands, can become uncheckable (the Massachusetts magistrates’ charge against Hutchinson).
positions/antinomianism/responses/0: Historic "antinomians" usually denied that they rejected holiness; they argued that holiness is the fruit, not the condition or evidence, of grace.
positions/antinomianism/responses/1: Modern grace preachers likewise affirm good works as the result of grace and argue that the label caricatures them.
positions/antinomianism/consequences/0: Forced Lutheran and Reformed churches to define the law’s role for believers.
positions/antinomianism/consequences/1: Contributed to the banishment of Hutchinson and Wheelwright and to Rhode Island’s religious diversity.
positions/antinomianism/consequences/2: Recurs in debates over free grace vs lordship salvation and "hyper-grace" teaching.
positions/theonomy/oneLine: God’s law, including the civil laws and penal sanctions of Moses, remains binding on all nations today except where the New Testament modifies it, and civil governments should be reconstructed according to it.
positions/theonomy/coreClaims/0: Christ did not abolish the law (Matt 5:17–19); every Old Testament stipulation continues unless revoked by later revelation.
positions/theonomy/coreClaims/1: Civil magistrates are bound to enforce God’s law, including its penalties, as "ministers of God" (Rom 13:4).
positions/theonomy/coreClaims/2: Every law-order is religious; neutrality is impossible, so the alternative to theonomy is autonomy.
positions/theonomy/coreClaims/3: The gospel will progressively transform cultures before Christ’s return (postmillennialism).
positions/theonomy/coreClaims/4: Change should come by regeneration, persuasion and lawful means, not by revolution.
positions/theonomy/origin: Rousas John Rushdoony, The Institutes of Biblical Law (1973), and Greg Bahnsen, Theonomy in Christian Ethics (1977), with Gary North and the Chalcedon Foundation (1965); antecedents in Puritan New England legal codes (e.g. John Cotton’s Moses his Judicials, 1636).
positions/theonomy/strongestArguments/0: Matthew 5:17–19 seems to affirm the continuing validity of "the least of these commandments".
positions/theonomy/strongestArguments/1: Deuteronomy 4:6–8 presents Israel’s statutes as a model of justice for the nations.
positions/theonomy/strongestArguments/2: If the state must legislate morality somehow, it is better to use God’s revealed standards than human preferences.
positions/theonomy/strongestObjections/0: Israel’s civil law belonged to a unique theocratic covenant; WCF 19.4 says it "expired together with the State of that people" (Barker and Godfrey, 1990).
positions/theonomy/strongestObjections/1: The New Testament never calls on states to enforce the Mosaic penalties; Jesus and Paul apply church discipline, not civil death penalties, to sinners (John 8; 1 Cor 5).
positions/theonomy/strongestObjections/2: Critics across the spectrum warn of coercion of religious minorities and dissenters, the very persecution Baptists and others suffered under confessional states.
positions/theonomy/responses/0: Theonomists answer that "general equity" means the abiding moral principle of each judicial law, which they seek to apply.
positions/theonomy/responses/1: They argue that coercion is limited because the Mosaic law itself restrains the state, and that theonomy is achieved by persuasion over generations.
positions/theonomy/consequences/0: Influenced the US Christian home-school movement and parts of the Religious Right, though few adopted full theonomy.
positions/theonomy/consequences/1: Prompted extensive Reformed critique and clarification of Westminster’s doctrine of the law.
positions/theonomy/consequences/2: Revived in some online "Christian nationalism" debates of the 2020s.
